entries.lesson_core_move: Interpret |H(j\omega)| as the frequency-dependent amplitude scaling applied by a continuous-time LTI system to sinusoidal inputs, using its variation over \omega to identify which components are attenuated, passed, or amplified.

sections.learning_goal: Define $|H(j\omega)|$ as the amplitude gain that a continuous-time LTI system applies at each frequency.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; keep the definition symbolic and compact.

question_policy.answer_format: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Define magnitude response as the frequency-by-frequency amplitude gain of a continuous-time LTI system and connect it to sinusoidal amplitude scaling.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with one sinusoidal input $x(t)=A\cos(\omega_0 t)$ and one gain value $|H(j\omega_0)|$; keep the focus on amplitude scaling and do not introduce phase or multiple frequencies.
paragraph_plan: Open with the meaning of $|H(j\omega)|$ as the amplitude gain applied at each frequency.
Show the base case $x(t)=A\cos(\omega_0 t)$ and state the scaling rule $A_{\text{out}}=|H(j\omega_0)|A_{\text{in}}$.
Define the three qualitative cases by comparing $|H(j\omega)|$ to 1: attenuated, passed, and amplified.
Close by previewing that the next sections will apply the same rule to one frequency, two frequencies, and then a whole curve.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the introduction tight: one definition, one base-case scaling rule, and one threshold rule. Do not introduce phase, curve reading, or multiple frequencies.

sections.learning_goal: Apply $|H(j\omega_0)|$ to one sinusoidal input to get the output amplitude.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; keep the worked example purely symbolic.

question_policy.answer_format: single numeric amplitude
question_policy.practice_question_model: If $x(t)=8\cos(5t)$ and $|H(j5)|=0.25$, what is the output amplitude?
distractor_plan: Use the unscaled input amplitude as a distractor.
Multiply by the wrong gain value or the reciprocal gain.
Add the gain to the amplitude instead of multiplying.
Use the gain from the wrong frequency.
Choose a nearby arithmetic result from a common multiplication mistake.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: An input $x(t)=6\cos(\omega_0 t)$ enters a system with $|H(j\omega_0)|=0.5$. Find the output amplitude.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the output amplitude equals the input amplitude multiplied by the magnitude gain at the same frequency.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the first numerical application of the definition: the student now multiplies a specific amplitude by a specific gain.
solution_step_plan: Identify the input amplitude and the frequency $\omega_0$.
Read the gain $|H(j\omega_0)|$ at that same frequency.
Multiply the input amplitude by the gain.
State the output amplitude and keep the same sinusoidal frequency.
practice_variation_axes: change the input amplitude
change the frequency label
change the gain value
switch between attenuation and amplification cases
keep the same structure but vary the arithmetic

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the worked example to one sinusoid and one gain value. The example should teach amplitude scaling only, not classification or curve reading.

sections.section_title: Classifying One Frequency as Attenuated, Passed, or Amplified
sections.learning_goal: Classify a single frequency as attenuated, passed, or amplified from its magnitude gain.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; keep the classification rule symbolic.

question_policy.answer_format: single classification label
question_policy.practice_question_model: If $|H(j\omega_0)|=1.3$, how is the component at $\omega_0$ classified?
distractor_plan: Use the adjacent class label instead of the correct one.
Treat $|H(j\omega_0)|=1$ as the wrong threshold.
Confuse the output amplitude with the class label.
Pick the class that matches a different frequency point.
Reverse attenuation and amplification.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: At $\omega_0$, a system has $|H(j\omega_0)|=0.75$. Classify the component at that frequency as attenuated, passed, or amplified.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Connect the gain threshold at 1 to the correct qualitative class.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This replaces arithmetic output scaling with the threshold rule for the three classes.
solution_step_plan: Compare $|H(j\omega_0)|$ to 1.
Use the rule $<1$ attenuated, $=1$ passed, $>1$ amplified.
Name the class and justify it with the comparison.
practice_variation_axes: values below 1
values equal to 1
values above 1
values close to the threshold
different frequency labels with the same rule

sections.handoff_notes: Center the example on the unity threshold. The later questions should probe the class label, not the output amplitude.

sections.section_title: Comparing Magnitude Response at Two Frequencies
sections.learning_goal: Compare two frequency points by their magnitude gains and identify which input component is more reduced or boosted.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; compare the two gains directly.

question_policy.answer_format: single comparative statement
question_policy.practice_question_model: A system has $|H(j\omega_1)|=0.8$ and $|H(j\omega_2)|=1.2$. Which frequency produces the larger output amplitude for the same input sinusoid?
distractor_plan: Swap the two frequencies in the comparison.
Compare the raw frequency labels instead of the gain values.
Ignore the unity threshold and choose the smaller gain as larger output.
Treat both frequencies as the same because they share one input.
Pick a class label instead of the requested comparison.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given $|H(j\omega_1)|=0.4$ and $|H(j\omega_2)|=1.6$, compare the output amplitudes for the same sinusoidal input at $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Compare the gains directly and conclude which frequency attenuates more and which amplifies more.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This extends the single-frequency classification to a two-frequency comparison.
solution_step_plan: Read both gain values at the two frequencies.
Compare them relative to 1 and to each other.
State which frequency is more attenuated and which is more amplified.
Translate that comparison into output-amplitude language.
practice_variation_axes: swap the gain order
make both gains below 1
make both gains above 1
include one gain equal to 1
use nearby numeric values so the comparison still matters

sections.handoff_notes: Make the comparison hinge on the gain values, not on the names of the frequencies. Keep the same input amplitude for both frequencies.

sections.section_title: Interpreting a Magnitude-Response Curve Across Frequency
sections.learning_goal: Read a magnitude-response curve and infer how the system treats different frequency bands.

image_policy.image_description_seed: A clean plot of $|H(j\omega)|$ versus $\omega$ with a bold horizontal reference line at 1 and a curve that is above 1 in one band, near 1 in another, and below 1 in another.
visual_elements: frequency bands above, at, and below unity
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use a single uncluttered instructional graph. Do not include phase, multiple panels, or decorative styling. The plot should make the above/equal/below-1 relation obvious.

question_policy.answer_format: single curve-interpretation or classification label
question_policy.practice_question_model: On a magnitude-response plot, which statement correctly describes the low-, middle-, and high-frequency regions relative to $|H(j\omega)|=1$?
distractor_plan: Focus on the slope or peak location instead of the height relative to 1.
Confuse low-frequency behavior with high-frequency behavior.
Ignore the unity reference line.
Infer phase behavior from the magnitude plot.
Misread a region that crosses 1 as staying entirely on one side of it.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Using the magnitude-response plot, identify which frequency regions are attenuated, passed, and amplified by comparing the curve to the unity line.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Read the whole curve relative to $|H(j\omega)|=1$ and map each frequency region to the correct class.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This moves from isolated frequency points to interpreting a full response curve across frequency.
solution_step_plan: Locate the unity reference line at $|H(j\omega)|=1$.
Scan the curve across low, mid, and high frequencies.
Label each region as attenuated, passed, or amplified according to its height relative to 1.
Summarize the band behavior in plain language.
practice_variation_axes: different curve shapes
one or multiple unity crossings
flat versus sloped regions
marked sample frequencies
different band widths and transition regions

sections.handoff_notes: The image is the task data here. Later practice should vary the curve while keeping the same unity-line reasoning.

entries.lesson_core_move: Interpret \angle H(j\omega) as the frequency-dependent phase shift applied to each sinusoidal input component when using frequency response to characterize LTI filter behavior.

sections.learning_goal: Introduce phase response as the frequency-dependent phase shift added to a sinusoidal component at $\omega_0$.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed.

question_policy.answer_format: not-applicable
question_policy.practice_question_model: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach that $\angle H(j\omega_0)$ is the phase offset contributed by the system to a sinusoid at frequency $\omega_0$.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use a single cosine input $x(t)=A\cos(\omega_0 t+\phi)$ so the learner tracks one frequency and one phase adjustment.
paragraph_plan: Connect phase response to the earlier frequency-response idea and state that the phase part of $H(j\omega)$ tells how the system shifts timing, not amplitude.
Show the single-sinusoid base case and write the output phase as the input phase plus $\angle H(j\omega_0)$ at the same frequency.
Close by naming the sign convention that later examples will use: positive phase advances the sinusoid and negative phase delays it.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this section short and formula-driven. Do not re-teach magnitude response or introduce comparison tasks yet; the goal is only to establish the phase-shift interpretation for one sinusoid.

sections.section_title: Reading \angle H(j\omega) at a Single Frequency
sections.learning_goal: Read a single complex frequency-response value and extract its phase angle as the phase shift at that frequency.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed.

question_policy.answer_format: Choose the phase shift at the specified frequency; write the angle in radians or as an equivalent lead/lag statement.
question_policy.practice_question_model: If $H(j4)=3e^{j\pi/4}$, what phase shift applies to a sinusoidal input at $\omega=4$?
distractor_plan: Use the magnitude $3$ instead of the angle.
Flip the sign of the phase angle.
Read the phase from the wrong frequency.
Confuse the phase shift with amplitude scaling.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given $H(j4)=3e^{j\pi/4}$, identify the phase shift experienced by a sinusoidal input at $\omega=4$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Extract the argument of the frequency-response value and state that the phase shift at $\omega=4$ is $\pi/4$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This adds one concrete frequency-response value but still asks only for the phase angle at a single frequency.
solution_step_plan: Read the complex value at the stated frequency.
Take its argument as the phase response.
State the phase shift directly and, if helpful, describe it as a lead.
practice_variation_axes: Change the frequency index.
Change the sign of the phase angle.
Present the response in exponential or polar form.
Ask for the phase as a lead-or-lag interpretation instead of a bare angle.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the worked example strictly symbolic. The later question writer should vary only the frequency value, the sign of the angle, or the polar/exponential form; do not introduce a graph or amplitude question here.

sections.section_title: Applying Phase Response to a Sinusoidal Component
sections.learning_goal: Apply the phase shift at one frequency to the phase of an input sinusoid and write the output sinusoid at the same frequency.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed.

question_policy.answer_format: Choose the output phase expression after applying the system phase shift to the input sinusoid.
question_policy.practice_question_model: If $x(t)=\cos(2t+\pi/4)$ and $\angle H(j2)=-\pi/6$, what is the output phase of the sinusoid?
distractor_plan: Subtract the system phase instead of adding it to the input phase.
Ignore the input phase and report only the system phase.
Use the phase from the wrong frequency.
Reverse the sign of the final phase.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: If $x(t)=\cos(2t+\pi/4)$ and $\angle H(j2)=-\pi/6$, write the steady-state output phase for the sinusoidal component.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Combine the input phase with the system phase shift to get the output phase $\pi/12$ at the same frequency.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This extends the single-frequency reading task by adding the input sinusoid's own phase, so the student must carry the phase shift through an actual output expression.
solution_step_plan: Identify the sinusoid frequency as $\omega_0=2$.
Read the system phase shift $\angle H(j2)=-\pi/6$.
Add the system phase shift to the input phase $\pi/4$.
Write the output sinusoid at the same frequency with the new phase.
practice_variation_axes: Change the input phase.
Change the sign or magnitude of $\angle H(j\omega_0)$.
Use a different single frequency.
Ask for the output phase only or for the full sinusoid expression.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the arithmetic light and the frequency fixed. The point is to apply the phase-response rule, not to revisit amplitude scaling or multi-frequency signals.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Positive and Negative Phase Shifts
sections.learning_goal: Interpret the sign of $\angle H(j\omega)$ as phase lead or lag for a sinusoidal component.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed.

question_policy.answer_format: Choose the correct lead-or-lag interpretation of the phase shift at the stated frequency.
question_policy.practice_question_model: If $\angle H(j3)=-\pi/2$, does the output at $\omega=3$ lead or lag the input, and by how much?
distractor_plan: Swap lead and lag.
Report the magnitude without the sign.
Treat the phase as an amplitude change.
Attach the phase to the wrong frequency.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: If $\angle H(j3)=\pi/5$ and $\angle H(j8)=-\pi/5$, describe the phase change at each frequency in terms of lead or lag.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Map positive phase to advance or lead and negative phase to delay or lag, using the two frequencies as contrasting cases.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This shifts from computing one output phase to interpreting what the sign means physically for the output timing.
solution_step_plan: Read the sign of each phase value.
State that a positive phase shift means the output leads or advances the input.
State that a negative phase shift means the output lags or delays the input.
Match each interpretation to its frequency.
practice_variation_axes: Change which frequency carries the positive or negative phase.
Ask for lead/lag language or advance/delay language.
Change the phase magnitude while preserving the sign logic.
Use one frequency instead of two when the sign interpretation is the only target.

sections.handoff_notes: Make the sign interpretation explicit. The worked example should not drift into amplitude or graph-reading language; it should train the learner to translate phase sign into timing language.

sections.learning_goal: Compare phase shifts at different frequencies to decide which component leads or lags more.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed.

question_policy.answer_format: Choose the comparison statement that correctly ranks the phase shifts across the given frequencies.
question_policy.practice_question_model: If $\angle H(j1)=\pi/6$ and $\angle H(j5)=-\pi/3$, which frequency component is more delayed?
distractor_plan: Choose the frequency with the larger absolute phase magnitude even when the sign points the other way.
Compare magnitude scaling instead of phase shift.
Swap the frequency labels.
Reverse lead/lag language.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: If $\angle H(j1)=\pi/6$ and $\angle H(j5)=-\pi/3$, determine which frequency component is more delayed and which is more advanced.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Use the phase values to rank the two frequencies by timing shift and identify the more advanced and more delayed component.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This extends single-frequency interpretation to a two-frequency comparison, so the student must compare phase values instead of reading one value in isolation.
solution_step_plan: List the phase shift at each frequency.
Compare the signs and magnitudes of the two values.
Decide which component is advanced more and which is delayed more.
State the comparison in words that match the phase response.
practice_variation_axes: Swap the order of the frequencies.
Use two positive, two negative, or mixed-sign phase values.
Ask for the frequency with larger lead, larger lag, or smaller absolute shift.
Ask for a ranking of timing shifts instead of a binary choice.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the comparison symbolic and explicit. The later writer should vary only the phase values and frequency labels; do not introduce a plot or any new frequency-response machinery.

entries.lesson_core_move: Evaluate low-frequency behavior by examining H(j\omega) as \omega approaches 0 and interpreting its magnitude and phase to decide how an LTI system scales, shifts, passes, or attenuates slowly varying inputs.

sections.learning_goal: Introduce low-frequency behavior as the near-DC limit of $H(j\omega)$ and connect it to slowly varying inputs.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the lesson is driven by symbolic limits and low-frequency interpretation of $H(j\omega)$.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image. Keep this step symbolic-only to minimize cognitive load.

question_policy.answer_format: not-applicable
question_policy.practice_question_model: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Teach that low-frequency behavior is read from $H(j\omega)$ as $\omega \to 0$, so the system's DC gain and DC phase tell you how slowly varying inputs are scaled and shifted.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with a constant-gain system where $H(j\omega)=K$ near $\omega=0$; then a slow sinusoid is approximately multiplied by $K$ and shifted by $\angle K$.
paragraph_plan: State the low-frequency question: what does the system do as $\omega \to 0$?
Explain that slowly varying inputs are well approximated by their near-DC sinusoidal components.
Connect the limit value $H(j0)$ to amplitude scaling.
Connect the angle of $H(j0)$ to phase shift or inversion.
Close by previewing the next examples: compute the limit, then read magnitude and phase separately.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Not used for the tutorial step.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Not used for the tutorial step.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Not used for the tutorial step.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the opening conceptual and DC-focused; do not move into filter classification or graph reading.

sections.section_title: Evaluating the Low-Frequency Limit of H(j\omega)
sections.learning_goal: Compute the low-frequency limit of a transfer function by evaluating $H(j\omega)$ as $\omega \to 0$.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the task is a symbolic limit evaluation at $\omega=0$.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image. The example should stay algebraic and compact.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic choices; one correct complex limit and low-frequency interpretation.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Compute $\lim_{\omega \to 0} H(j\omega)$ for a simple rational transfer function and choose the correct DC value.
distractor_plan: Use the value at a nonzero frequency instead of the limit at $\omega=0$.
Swap numerator and denominator when evaluating the DC value.
Report only the magnitude and ignore the complex value.
Keep the $\omega$ terms instead of taking the limit.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Not used for an example step.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Not used for an example step.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given $H(j\omega)=\frac{2-j\omega}{4+j\omega}$, evaluate $\lim_{\omega\to 0}H(j\omega)$ and state the low-frequency gain and phase.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the limit is found by direct substitution at $\omega=0$ and then interpreted as the DC gain and DC phase.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This turns the tutorial's conceptual rule into a concrete limit computation for a rational frequency response with a simple DC value.
solution_step_plan: Substitute $\omega=0$ into the numerator and denominator to get the DC value.
Write the limit as the complex constant $H(j0)$.
Separate the result into magnitude and phase.
Interpret the magnitude as the slow-signal scaling factor and the phase as the low-frequency shift.
practice_variation_axes: Change the constant numerator and denominator terms.
Use a rational function that simplifies cleanly at $\omega=0$.
Ask for the limiting value before the interpretation.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the algebra minimal and make the DC-limit computation the only new skill.

sections.learning_goal: Use $|H(j0)|$ to decide whether slow sinusoidal components are attenuated, passed, or amplified.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the interpretation depends only on the symbolic gain value at $\omega=0$.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image. Keep the interpretation numeric and symbolic.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic choices; one correct amplitude classification for a slow sinusoid.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given a low-frequency gain $|H(j0)|$, choose the correct attenuation, pass, or amplification statement for a slowly varying sinusoid.
distractor_plan: Confuse gain less than 1 with amplification.
Classify based on phase instead of magnitude.
Treat the exact gain value as a percentage without scaling the input.
Use the wrong frequency and ignore the low-frequency limit.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Not used for an example step.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Not used for an example step.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Suppose $H(j0)=\frac{1}{2}$. For a slowly varying sinusoidal input, decide whether the system attenuates, passes, or amplifies the component and by what factor.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that low-frequency magnitude less than 1 means attenuation and that the output amplitude is multiplied by the gain.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This reuses the low-frequency value from the limit step but shifts the task from computing the limit to interpreting its magnitude.
solution_step_plan: Read the low-frequency gain from $H(j0)$.
Compare the magnitude with 1 to classify the behavior.
State the output amplitude scaling factor.
Connect the result back to slowly varying input components.
practice_variation_axes: Change the low-frequency gain to another value below 1.
Change the input amplitude while keeping the gain fixed.
Ask for the classification rather than the exact output expression.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the same DC gain logic, but make the magnitude classification the only decision the learner has to make.

sections.learning_goal: Use $\angle H(j0)$ to determine the low-frequency phase shift applied to slow sinusoidal components.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the task is to infer phase shift from the sign of the low-frequency gain.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image. This example should remain symbolic and phase-focused.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic choices; one correct phase-shift and inversion description.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given a negative real value of $H(j0)$, choose the correct low-frequency phase shift and output description.
distractor_plan: Use $0$ phase instead of the $\pi$ phase implied by a negative real gain.
Confuse the magnitude with the phase shift.
Describe a time delay when the limit is just a negative constant.
Ignore the sign and report only the amplitude scale.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Not used for an example step.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Not used for an example step.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Suppose $H(j0)=-2$. For a slowly varying sinusoidal input, determine the low-frequency phase shift and describe the resulting output component.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that a negative real low-frequency gain has phase $\pi$ and therefore inverts the sinusoid while scaling its amplitude by 2.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This adds the phase interpretation wrinkle by using a negative DC gain, so magnitude stays simple while the sign forces a $\pi$ shift.
solution_step_plan: Read the low-frequency gain as a negative real constant.
Convert the negative sign into a phase shift of $\pi$.
State the output amplitude scaling factor.
Describe the resulting inversion of the slowly varying sinusoid.
practice_variation_axes: Change the sign of $H(j0)$ while keeping the magnitude simple.
Vary the input sinusoid's phase offset.
Ask for the phase interpretation and the output description together.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the sign-to-phase connection explicit and do not drift into high-frequency behavior.

sections.section_title: Deciding How Slowly Varying Inputs Change Through the System
sections.learning_goal: Combine the low-frequency gain and phase to predict how a slowly varying input is scaled and shifted.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the final decision depends on the symbolic low-frequency gain and phase only.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate an image. Keep the final decision symbolic and compact.

question_policy.answer_format: Five symbolic choices; one correct combined gain-and-phase description.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given a slowly varying sinusoid and a low-frequency limit $H(j0)$, choose the correct combined scaling and phase description.
distractor_plan: Omit the phase shift and report only the amplitude scaling.
Omit the amplitude scaling and report only the sign of the gain.
Treat the input as high-frequency instead of slowly varying.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Not used for an example step.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Not used for an example step.

solution_step_plan: Read the low-frequency gain and separate its magnitude and sign.

Apply the magnitude as the amplitude scaling factor.

entries.lesson_core_move: Evaluate high-frequency limits of |H(j\omega)| and \angle H(j\omega) to predict how an LTI system passes, attenuates, or phase-shifts rapidly varying sinusoidal components.

sections.learning_goal: Define high-frequency behavior as the asymptotic response of $|H(j\omega)|$ and $\angle H(j\omega)$ and connect those limits to the fate of rapid sinusoidal inputs.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; keep the step symbolic.

question_policy.answer_format: No questions in the tutorial step.
question_policy.practice_question_model: No practice question for the tutorial.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Show that when $\omega$ is large, the only information that matters is the limit of $|H(j\omega)|$ and $\angle H(j\omega)$, because those limits determine whether fast sinusoidal components are passed, attenuated, or phase-shifted.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use a simple first-order response such as $H(j\omega)=\frac{1}{1+j\omega}$ so the student sees the high-frequency pattern: the magnitude shrinks while the phase settles to a constant lag.
paragraph_plan: State the question: what happens to an LTI system when the input sinusoid is very fast.
Define high-frequency behavior as the asymptotic limits of $|H(j\omega)|$ and $\angle H(j\omega)$ as $\omega\to\infty$.
Connect those limits to the same-frequency output rule from frequency response so the learner sees that only gain and phase change.
Use one simple rational example to show that the dominant powers of $j\omega$ control the limit.
Transition to the worked examples that compute magnitude limits, phase limits, dominant-power simplifications, and output prediction.

sections.learning_goal: Compute a high-frequency magnitude limit from a rational transfer function and interpret it as attenuation, passage, or amplification of rapid sinusoidal components.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the step is a symbolic limit computation.

question_policy.answer_format: Single-answer multiple-choice with five symbolic choices for the high-frequency magnitude limit.
question_policy.practice_question_model: What is $\lim_{\omega\to\infty}|H(j\omega)|$ for $H(j\omega)=\frac{3j\omega+2}{2j\omega-5}$?
distractor_plan: Use the constant terms instead of the leading terms.
Invert the numerator/denominator ratio.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Evaluate $\lim_{\omega\to\infty}|H(j\omega)|$ for $H(j\omega)=\frac{3j\omega+2}{2j\omega-5}$ and decide whether very high-frequency components are attenuated, passed, or amplified.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Keep only the leading $j\omega$ terms, reduce the expression to the dominant coefficient ratio, and use the resulting magnitude to classify the rapid sinusoid as amplified rather than attenuated.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: First explicit limit computation after the tutorial; stay on magnitude only and postpone phase to the next section.
solution_step_plan: Write the high-frequency approximation by keeping only the leading terms in the numerator and denominator.
Take the magnitude of the dominant coefficient ratio.
State the asymptotic gain and interpret it as high-frequency amplification.
practice_variation_axes: Change the leading coefficient ratio while keeping the degrees matched.
Move the limit above or below $1$ so the answer is amplification or attenuation.
Include lower-order clutter that should be ignored at high frequency.
Swap signs in the leading terms without changing the magnitude.

sections.handoff_notes: Stay in symbolic algebra and end with a clear pass, attenuate, or amplify statement.

sections.learning_goal: Compute a high-frequency phase limit from a rational transfer function and interpret it as the asymptotic phase shift on a rapid sinusoid.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the step is a symbolic phase-limit computation.

question_policy.answer_format: Single-answer multiple-choice with five symbolic choices for the high-frequency phase limit.
question_policy.practice_question_model: What is $\lim_{\omega\to\infty}\angle H(j\omega)$ for $H(j\omega)=\frac{2-j\omega}{1+j\omega}$?
distractor_plan: Use the magnitude limit instead of the phase limit.
Flip the sign of the limiting phase angle.
Read only one leading factor and answer $-\pi/2$.
Confuse the numerator's angle with the denominator's angle.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Evaluate $\lim_{\omega\to\infty}\angle H(j\omega)$ for $H(j\omega)=\frac{1-j\omega}{1+j\omega}$ and interpret the asymptotic phase shift on a rapid sinusoid.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Use the high-frequency angles of the leading numerator and denominator terms to show that the phase tends to a constant $-\pi$ shift, which flips the sign of the rapid sinusoid.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Keep the same high-frequency setting but switch from amplitude to phase so the learner sees what changes and what stays fixed.
solution_step_plan: Identify the leading terms in the numerator and denominator as $\omega$ grows.
Read off the asymptotic angles of those leading terms.
Subtract the denominator phase from the numerator phase to get the constant phase limit.
Interpret the result as an inverted high-frequency sinusoid.
practice_variation_axes: Change the sign pattern in the leading terms.
Use phase answers in radians rather than degrees.
Test whether the learner can distinguish $\pi$ from $-\pi$.
Include a distractor that confuses phase with magnitude.

sections.handoff_notes: Treat phase as a constant asymptotic shift on the same-frequency output.

sections.section_title: Using Dominant Powers of j\omega in High-Frequency Limits
sections.learning_goal: Use dominant powers of $j\omega$ to strip away lower-order terms and read the high-frequency magnitude limit quickly.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the step is a symbolic dominant-power simplification.

question_policy.answer_format: Single-answer multiple-choice with five symbolic choices for the asymptotic magnitude limit.
question_policy.practice_question_model: What is the high-frequency magnitude limit of $H(j\omega)=\frac{2(j\omega)^2+3}{5(j\omega)^3-j\omega+1}$?
distractor_plan: Compare the constant terms instead of the highest powers.
Treat the lower-order numerator terms as if they controlled the limit.
Claim a finite nonzero constant limit even though the denominator has one extra power.
Confuse the dominant-power shortcut with a full expansion.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Use dominant powers of $j\omega$ to evaluate the high-frequency magnitude limit of $H(j\omega)=\frac{3(j\omega)^2-2j\omega+1}{(j\omega)^3+4(j\omega)^2-5}$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Factor out the highest powers of $j\omega$, cancel what survives, and show that the extra denominator power forces the magnitude to go to $0$.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Add lower-order clutter and a degree mismatch so the dominant-power argument does all the work.
solution_step_plan: Factor the highest power of $j\omega$ from the numerator and denominator.
Cancel the common highest power and isolate the leftover power gap.
Read the magnitude limit from the remaining factor.
State why the lower-order terms do not affect the high-frequency result.
practice_variation_axes: Change the degree gap between numerator and denominator.
Hide the dominant terms behind extra lower-order clutter.
Vary the leading coefficients while keeping the power count the key step.
Ask for a zero limit versus a finite nonzero limit.

sections.handoff_notes: Make the dominant-power cancellation explicit; do not expand the lower-order terms.

sections.section_title: Predicting Rapid-Sinusoid Output from High-Frequency Gain and Phase
sections.learning_goal: Combine asymptotic gain and phase to predict the output waveform of a rapid sinusoid.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the step is a symbolic output-prediction problem.

question_policy.answer_format: Single-answer multiple-choice with five symbolic choices for the approximate output waveform.
question_policy.practice_question_model: If $x(t)=4\cos(\omega_0 t+\pi/8)$ and $H(j\omega)\to-\tfrac{1}{2}$ as $\omega\to\infty$, what is the approximate output for very large $\omega_0$?
distractor_plan: Keep the input amplitude but miss the scaling factor from the high-frequency gain.
Apply the phase shift with the wrong sign.
Change the output frequency instead of keeping $\omega_0$.
Forget to add the input phase to the system phase.
Treat the high-frequency limit as if it were a low-frequency response.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For very large $\omega_0$, predict the output of $x(t)=3\cos(\omega_0 t-\pi/6)$ when the high-frequency limit of $H(j\omega)$ is $-2$.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Combine a high-frequency gain of $2$ with a phase shift of $\pi$ to write the output as a cosine with doubled amplitude and inverted phase.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Move from asymptotic analysis to actual output prediction for a rapid sinusoid.
solution_step_plan: Read the high-frequency gain and phase from the limit of $H(j\omega)$.
Apply the sinusoid output rule $A\cos(\omega_0 t+\phi)\mapsto A|H|\cos(\omega_0 t+\phi+\angle H)$.
Substitute the input amplitude and phase.
Simplify the result to a standard cosine form and classify the component as passed, attenuated, or amplified.
practice_variation_axes: Change the input amplitude and initial phase.
Vary the gain above or below $1$.
Switch between phase inversion and quarter-cycle lag.
Require equivalent output forms that differ only by a phase rewrite.

sections.handoff_notes: Finish by converting the asymptotic gain and phase into the output cosine form.

entries.lesson_core_move: Identify low-pass behavior in H(j\omega) by comparing its magnitude at low and high frequencies and interpreting strong low-frequency passage with high-frequency attenuation as the system preserving slow sinusoidal components while suppressing rapid ones.

sections.learning_goal: Define low-pass behavior as a frequency-dependent magnitude pattern where $|H(j\omega)|$ is larger at low frequencies than at high frequencies.

tutorial_outline.base_case: Start with one low-frequency sinusoid and one high-frequency sinusoid passed through the same system, and compare their output amplitudes.
paragraph_plan: State the low-pass definition in terms of comparing $|H(j\omega)|$ at small and large $\omega$.
Show the common case where $|H(j\omega)|$ is near 1 at low frequency and much smaller at high frequency.

sections.learning_goal: Recognize low-pass behavior from a pair of magnitudes that show strong low-frequency passage and weak high-frequency transmission.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; use a symbolic comparison of low- and high-frequency magnitudes.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not introduce a graph; the worked example should stay text-only.

question_policy.answer_format: Single-correct multiple-choice classification with five text choices.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given $|H(j\omega_{\text{low}})| \approx 1$ and $|H(j\omega_{\text{high}})| \ll 1$, ask which statement best describes how the system treats slow versus fast components.
distractor_plan: Swap the roles of low and high frequency and make the system look high-pass.
Describe the system as all-pass by claiming both frequencies are preserved equally.
Claim the response is phase-only and does not change amplitude.
Claim the comparison is inconclusive even though the low-frequency gain is much larger.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A system has $|H(j\omega_{\text{low}})| = 0.95$ at a small frequency and $|H(j\omega_{\text{high}})| = 0.08$ at a much larger frequency. What does that tell you about how the system treats slow and rapid sinusoidal components?
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that low-frequency components are passed with little attenuation while high-frequency components are strongly attenuated, so the system is low-pass.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Moves from the general definition to a concrete numerical comparison that the learner must classify.
solution_step_plan: Identify which magnitude corresponds to the low frequency and which corresponds to the high frequency.
Compare their sizes and note that the low-frequency magnitude is near 1 while the high-frequency magnitude is much smaller.
Translate that contrast into the fate of the corresponding sinusoidal components.
State the classification: the system behaves like a low-pass filter.
practice_variation_axes: Change the actual magnitude values while keeping the same low-vs-high pattern.
Swap which frequency is labeled low or high to force the learner to track frequency, not just size.
Vary whether the low-frequency magnitude is exactly 1, slightly below 1, or slightly above 1.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the prompt narrow and numerical. The later question writer should ask for a classification from the low-vs-high magnitude contrast, not for a plot reading.

sections.learning_goal: Read a small $|H(j\omega)|$ value at high frequency as attenuation of the corresponding rapid sinusoidal component.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; the task is to interpret a small high-frequency gain symbolically.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Keep the example free of plots or diagrams; the magnitude value is enough.

question_policy.answer_format: Single-correct multiple-choice classification with five text choices.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given a high-frequency sinusoid and a small value of $|H(j\omega)|$, ask what happens to its amplitude and how that supports a low-pass interpretation.
distractor_plan: Turn the small high-frequency gain into a high-pass claim.
Treat the small gain as a phase-only shift.
Claim the component is passed essentially unchanged because it is still present.
Apply the attenuation to the wrong frequency region or claim all frequencies are reduced equally.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: At $\omega = 40$, the magnitude response is $|H(j40)| = 0.05$. What happens to a sinusoidal input at that frequency?
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the output sinusoid keeps the same frequency but has much smaller amplitude, which means the high-frequency component is suppressed.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Instead of comparing two frequencies, this example isolates the high-frequency end and asks for the effect on one fast component.
solution_step_plan: Identify the input as a high-frequency sinusoid.
Use the small gain to infer strong amplitude reduction.
State that the output frequency stays the same while the amplitude shrinks.
Connect that attenuation to low-pass behavior.
practice_variation_axes: Vary the high-frequency gain from small to very small.
Change the input description from one sinusoid to a rapid component inside a larger signal.
Keep the reasoning focused on amplitude reduction rather than phase.

sections.handoff_notes: The later writer should keep this a gain-reading problem, not a graph interpretation or phase-shift problem.

sections.learning_goal: Use a direct comparison between $|H(j\omega_{\text{low}})|$ and $|H(j\omega_{\text{high}})|$ to decide whether the system is low-pass.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; compare two symbolic magnitude values.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not add a response curve; the comparison should stay entirely in text.

question_policy.answer_format: Single-correct multiple-choice classification with five text choices.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given two magnitudes at low and high frequency, ask which frequency is passed more strongly and what filter behavior that implies.
distractor_plan: Reverse the comparison and call the system high-pass.
Treat the system as all-pass because both values are nonzero.
Interpret the numbers as phase information rather than magnitude information.
Say no conclusion is possible even though the low-frequency magnitude is much larger.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: A system has $|H(j\omega_{\text{low}})| = 1.1$ and $|H(j\omega_{\text{high}})| = 0.2$. Which frequency is passed more strongly, and what filter behavior does that imply?
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the low-frequency gain is much larger than the high-frequency gain, so the response is low-pass.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This example forces a side-by-side comparison rather than reading a single frequency value.
solution_step_plan: Compare the two magnitudes numerically.
Interpret the larger low-frequency gain as stronger passage of slow components.
Interpret the smaller high-frequency gain as attenuation of rapid components.
Conclude low-pass behavior from the contrast.
practice_variation_axes: Make the two magnitudes closer together or farther apart.
Change whether one value is above 1, below 1, or approximately 1.
Reverse the labels in distractors to test whether the learner tracks frequency ordering.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the solution centered on relative magnitude, not on absolute gain alone.

sections.section_title: Interpreting Low-Pass Behavior for Sinusoidal Components
sections.learning_goal: Apply the low-pass rule to a composite sinusoidal input and describe which component dominates the output.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image needed; interpret a composite sinusoidal input with symbolic magnitudes.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Keep the example text-only; the learner should reason from the stated frequencies and gains.

question_policy.answer_format: Single-correct multiple-choice classification with five text choices.
question_policy.practice_question_model: Given a composite input with one slow and one fast sinusoid, ask which component remains prominent after a low-pass system.
distractor_plan: Preserve the fast component and suppress the slow one.
Claim both components are scaled by the same amount.
Treat the output as a phase-only change with no amplitude effect.
Ignore the frequency dependence and describe the input as unchanged.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: An input is $x(t) = \cos(\omega_{\text{slow}} t) + \cos(\omega_{\text{fast}} t)$ with $\omega_{\text{slow}}$ small and $\omega_{\text{fast}}$ large. If $|H(j\omega_{\text{slow}})| \approx 1$ and $|H(j\omega_{\text{fast}})| \approx 0.1$, what does the output look like component by component?
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the slow component remains prominent while the fast component is strongly reduced, so the output preserves the slowly varying part of the input.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Extends the same low-pass rule from one sinusoid or one comparison to a composite input with multiple frequencies.
solution_step_plan: Separate the input into slow and fast sinusoidal components.
Apply the low-frequency gain to the slow component and the high-frequency gain to the fast component.
Describe the output as dominated by the slow component because it is passed more strongly.
State the interpretation in words: low-pass behavior preserves slow variations and suppresses rapid variations.
practice_variation_axes: Change the number of sinusoidal components in the input.
Vary whether the attenuated component is merely smaller or nearly removed.
Swap the labels slow and fast to ensure the learner uses frequency, not signal order.

sections.handoff_notes: Do not ask for an exact waveform. The task is qualitative component-by-component interpretation.

entries.lesson_core_move: Classify high-pass behavior for an LTI filter from its magnitude response by comparing |H(j\omega)| at low and high frequencies and identifying low-frequency attenuation with high-frequency passage.

sections.learning_goal: Use the low- and high-frequency ends of $|H(j\omega)|$ to decide whether a filter is low-pass, high-pass, or neither.

sections.section_title: Classifying Neither Low-Pass Nor High-Pass Behavior
sections.learning_goal: Reject low-pass and high-pass labels when the low- and high-frequency ends do not show a one-sided passband pattern.

image_policy.image_description_seed: A magnitude-response plot with low- and high-frequency ends at similar sub-unity gain and a central hump above 1, so the response is not low-pass or high-pass.
visual_elements: middle region that differs from the ends
single hump or notch that makes the response neither low-pass nor high-pass
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Make the two ends look comparable so the student must reject both passband labels. Keep the middle feature obvious but secondary to the end comparison.

question_policy.answer_format: single classification label

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For the displayed magnitude-response curve, decide whether the filter is low-pass, high-pass, or neither.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the low- and high-frequency ends do not support either passband label, so the filter is neither low-pass nor high-pass.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This keeps the same end-comparison rule but uses a response whose ends do not separate into low-pass or high-pass behavior.
solution_step_plan: Read the low-frequency and high-frequency ends of the plot.
Notice that the ends are about the same height rather than showing a one-sided passage pattern.
Reject both low-pass and high-pass labels on that basis.
State that the correct classification is neither.

low and high ends both above 1
a middle bump or notch that does not change the end comparison
responses that look like band-pass or band-stop shapes
different plateau levels with similar low and high ends

sections.handoff_notes: The point is to reject both passband labels using the low/high ends. The middle shape should support that conclusion, not replace it.
